messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: QA Engineer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Visual (Fire/Flames): Fire or flames, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Carlos, a seventy-five-year-old QA engineer of Latin American descent, had always prided himself on his attention to detail. For decades, his job required him to scan software code for the smallest inconsistencies, the kind of errors that could bring an entire system down. He brought that same meticulousness to every part of his life, especially after retiring from full-time work and taking on a few consulting projects from home. But the wildfire that swept through his neighborhood two years ago changed the way he saw everything. What had once been a virtue—his careful, methodical mind—had become a trap.

The fire had started in the hills on a dry, windy October afternoon. Carlos remembered the heat, the orange glow on the horizon, the smell of pine and eucalyptus burning long before the evacuation order came. He and his wife had packed quickly, and they made it out safely, their house spared by a last-minute shift in the wind. But in the weeks and months that followed, Carlos could not stop turning the event over in his head. He dwelled endlessly on what he had done wrong—why hadn’t he filled the gutters with water sooner? Why had he waited to grab the photo albums? He replayed the hours before the evacuation, running through every decision, convinced he could have prevented the whole ordeal if he had just acted more quickly, if he had checked the weather forecast more carefully that morning. The rumination became a habit: every time he smelled woodsmoke from a neighbor’s fireplace, or saw the flicker of a candle, his mind would plunge back into that afternoon, sorting through the should-haves and could-haves.

He tried to push the thoughts out of his mind. Whenever a memory surfaced—the crackling sound, the orange sky, the acrid taste in the air—he would force himself to think of something else, anything else. He would turn on the television, walk into another room, or focus intently on a code defect. But the suppression never lasted. The memories kept returning, unbidden, and with them came a tightness in his chest, a racing heart, a tremor in his hands. The physical reactions were automatic and overwhelming. A whiff of smoke from a distant barbecue could leave him breathless and dizzy for minutes. He became hypervigilant, watching for any sign of fire: scanning the sky for haze, checking the weather app obsessively for wind speeds and low humidity, noting the direction of the breeze whenever he stepped outside. The slightest unexpected noise—a car backfiring, a door slamming—made him jump. He had never been a jumpy person, but now his body seemed to be bracing for disaster at all times.

These reactions infiltrated his work. At his home office, he kept the window blinds closed so he wouldn’t be distracted by the color of the sky. He avoided working on days when the weather felt too similar to that October afternoon—warm, dry, with a gusting wind. When a colleague casually mentioned a planned burn in the nearby forest, Carlos ended the call abruptly, his hands shaking. He stopped going to the hardware store where the faint smell of gas and cleaning products reminded him of the emergency supplies he had packed. His wife noticed he no longer wanted to light candles at dinner, something they had done for decades. He would not explain why. He simply said it was better to keep the house dark.

What finally brought Carlos to seek help was a single moment of recognition. During a routine smoke alarm test at the office he visited for quarterly meetings, the shrill beep triggered a flashback so vivid he had to leave the building and sit on the curb, gasping. His boss suggested he take a leave of absence. At home that night, his wife told him, gently, that she could not keep living around his unspoken terror. Carlos realized then that he had been trying to outrun a fire that had already happened—and that the real damage was not to his house, but to the quiet, steady life he had built. He wanted to stop dwelling on what he had done wrong. He wanted to stop feeling like his own body was sounding a false alarm. But he was afraid that if he let himself fully remember the smoke and the flames, he would never find his way back.
